explainers.title: What is an ERP?
explainers.takeaway: An ERP keeps every team on the same records.
explainers.dek: The Coffee Company's spreadsheets disagree, and a cafe order goes wrong. Ishita learns what an ERP is, and who makes ERPNext.
explainers.so_far: The Coffee Company roasts beans and sells them to cafes and online. Its three spreadsheets disagree.

panels.caption: The Coffee Company roasts coffee beans, packs them and sells them to cafes and online. Ishita started it. It's 11 PM, and she is checking three spreadsheets.
Three sheets: orders, stock and invoices.
panels.thought: Stock says we still have the Ethiopian roast. Invoices say we sold the last bag.

panels.caption: Same night. Raju, who sells to the cafes, is on the phone.
panels.left_bubble: The Ethiopian roast? By tomorrow? Consider it done!

panels.thought: Wait. The roastery sold the last bag on Tuesday. Nobody told the stock sheet.

panels.caption: Next morning. The cafe's order can't be filled.
panels.thought: Three sheets and Raju's phone. Nobody sees the whole picture.

panels.caption: Raju calls his oldest friend.
panels.left_bubble: You use that business software every day. Can you come by and fix our mess?

panels.caption: His friend is The Frappe Guy.
panels.right_bubble: I'll come over this afternoon and look first. Ask Ishita to bring the three sheets.

panels.caption: That afternoon, at the counter.
panels.left_bubble: Raju says you can fix this mess.
Here. Orders, stock, invoices.
panels.right_bubble: Coffee first. Then walk me through them.

panels.left_bubble: So, can you fix it?
panels.right_bubble: The usual fix is an ERP: one system where every team works on the same records.

panels.caption: Salman, who designs the coffee bags, is listening.
panels.left_bubble: Sorry, silly question. What does ERP even mean?

panels.right_bubble: Not silly. It stands for enterprise resource planning. Forget the name. Think: one shared record for everyone.

panels.caption: Enter the order once. Every team reads the same record.
panels.diagram_labels:
# Raju's cafe order
- Stock: bags promised
- Invoice: made from it
- Accounts: money owed
- Ishita: sees everything

panels.left_bubble: So last night, Raju's phone would have shown the roast was sold out.
panels.right_bubble: For everyone, at the same moment.

panels.left_bubble: Which ERP would you pick?
panels.right_bubble: The one I use every day: ERPNext. A company called Frappe makes it.

panels.left_bubble: Frappe, ERPNext. Why two names?
panels.right_bubble: Frappe is the company. ERPNext is what it makes. Like The Coffee Company and its Ethiopian roast.

panels.left_bubble: What would it cover for us?
panels.right_bubble: Selling to cafes, buying beans, stock, accounts and projects. Frappe HR adds payroll when you're ready.
One catch. An ERP changes how every team works. Frappe says any ERP is complex to set up alone.

panels.thought: Every team, every record, for years. Then I need to know who is behind it.

panels.left_bubble: Before I trust them with my whole company: who are these people?
panels.right_bubble: Fair question. And it's a good story.

explainers.title: Who is behind this?
explainers.takeaway: Before you pick an ERP, look at who builds it and how.
explainers.dek: Before Ishita trusts ERPNext with her company, she wants to know who builds it and how they work.
explainers.so_far: The sheets disagree. The Frappe Guy says an ERP would put every team on one record. Ishita wants to know who makes ERPNext.

panels.caption: So far: The Coffee Company's sheets disagree. The Frappe Guy says an ERP would put every team on one record. Ishita wants to know who makes ERPNext.

panels.left_bubble: Why does the maker matter so much? I never ask who makes my phone apps.

panels.right_bubble: You can delete a phone app. An ERP would hold your orders, stock and accounts for years.

panels.left_bubble: And if it stops fitting how we work?
panels.right_bubble: Then someone has to change it. So you want to know who that is.

panels.left_bubble: Like visiting a bean farm before a long contract.
panels.right_bubble: Same test.
Then here's the farm. Frappe began with a problem like yours.

panels.caption: Frappe's founder is Rushabh Mehta. His family's furniture factory was struggling with a bad ERP, built by a local company.
panels.thought: Stuck with software someone else built.

panels.left_bubble: So what did he do?
panels.right_bubble: He started writing his own.

panels.caption: First the side project, then the company, then the product's name.
panels.diagram_labels:
# 2005
- A side project begins
# 2008
- Frappe is founded
# 2010
- ERPNext gets its name

panels.caption: Frappe's co-founders: Nabin Hait, Mohammad Umair Sayed and Prakash Hodage.
panels.left_bubble: So it's not one person's side project anymore.
Then who decides what gets built and fixed? A boss somewhere?

panels.right_bubble: No reporting managers. People choose their own work and set their own pay.

panels.left_bubble: Then who decides?
panels.right_bubble: They decide together, democratically, under a written constitution.
Frappe calls itself a collective: a company its people run together. People first, money second.

panels.left_bubble: No managers, for software my company runs on? That sounds risky.
panels.right_bubble: It's unusual. Don't take my word for it. They publish how they work.

panels.left_bubble: So I visit the bean farm. Check the builders, not only the brochure.
panels.right_bubble: That's the test. Then ask to meet a customer your size.
And they publish more than that. ERPNext's code is open for anyone to read.

panels.caption: Across the room, Sara, who runs finance, heard all of it.
panels.thought: Anyone can read it? Nobody gives things away. What's the catch?

explainers.title: Why it is open source
explainers.takeaway: You can read, run and change ERPNext's code.
explainers.dek: Sara runs finance and trusts what she can check. What is code, and why would anyone let you read it?
explainers.so_far: Ishita checked who makes ERPNext. The Frappe Guy says anyone can read its code.

panels.caption: So far: Ishita checked who makes ERPNext. The Frappe Guy says anyone can read its code. Over lunch, Sara, who runs finance, wants proof.

panels.left_bubble: You said anyone can read their code. What is code, and why should finance care?

panels.right_bubble: Code is the written instructions software follows. Every screen and every total in ERPNext comes from it.

panels.left_bubble: Like a recipe for our roast?
panels.right_bubble: Exactly. The recipe behind every number you report.

panels.left_bubble: We keep our roast recipe secret.
panels.right_bubble: So do most software makers. That's called closed source.

panels.caption: ERPNext is open source.
panels.diagram_labels:
# Closed source
- Only the maker reads
- Only the maker changes
# Open source
- Anyone can read it
- Anyone can run it
- Anyone can change it

panels.left_bubble: Open because they promise?
panels.right_bubble: Because of its licence: the written rules on what anyone may do with the code.

panels.caption: ERPNext was put under an open licence early on. Its code has been online since 2009.

panels.left_bubble: Why would anyone give their recipe away?
panels.right_bubble: Frappe's view: open software is something everyone can use, and it shouldn't tie its users down.

panels.left_bubble: All of it, or only a taste?
panels.right_bubble: All of it. No feature is held back.

panels.left_bubble: So what's the catch? Is it free?
panels.right_bubble: The software has no licence fee. The money goes into setting it up and running it.

panels.caption: At the next table: Joseph, who runs tech.
panels.left_bubble: I've read their code. Twice. For fun.
I'm never reading code.
panels.right_bubble: You don't have to. Open means someone you trust can check it for you. Like Joseph.

panels.left_bubble: So we can read it, run it and change it.
panels.right_bubble: Yes. It's yours to use and change.

panels.thought: Readable today. But what if we want out in a few years?

explainers.title: What if we want to leave?
explainers.takeaway: Nobody can lock you in. You still need good people.
explainers.dek: Sara asks what happens if they ever want out: lock-in, setting it up, partners and where the system runs.
explainers.so_far: ERPNext's code is open. Anyone can read it, run it and change it.

panels.caption: So far: ERPNext's code is open. Anyone can read it, run it and change it. Sara is thinking a few years ahead.

panels.left_bubble: Say we run on ERPNext for years, then want to leave. What happens?

panels.right_bubble: Leaving any ERP is work. But nobody can lock you in.

panels.left_bubble: Lock us in? How?
panels.right_bubble: Lock-in: only the maker can run or change your system, so leaving means starting over.

panels.caption: Open code means no lock-in.
panels.diagram_labels:
# Locked in
- Your records
- Run by one maker
- Leaving means starting over
# Open
- Your records in ERPNext
- Any team runs it
- Switch teams, same system

panels.left_bubble: Years of cafe orders, stuck with one maker.
panels.right_bubble: That's lock-in. With open code, another team can pick up the same system.

panels.left_bubble: Another team? Who's the first team?
panels.right_bubble: Whoever sets ERPNext up for you.
An ERP has to be set up around how you work. That's called implementation.

panels.left_bubble: Set up how? Give me our example.
panels.right_bubble: Your warehouses, your cafe price list, who approves a bean order.

panels.left_bubble: That's a lot of decisions. Who makes them with us?

panels.right_bubble: Usually a Frappe Partner: a company trained and certified to set it up and support it.

panels.left_bubble: And if we don't get on with our partner?
panels.right_bubble: You can change partners. It takes work, so keep the admin login and every change they make in your name.

panels.left_bubble: So the system is ours.
Set up where, though? Where does it actually run? On Joseph's laptop?
My laptop already runs three sheets and a cat video. No.

panels.right_bubble: Software like this runs on a computer that's always on and looked after. That's hosting.

panels.left_bubble: So the counter, the roastery and Raju's phone all reach the same system?
panels.right_bubble: Yes. The same records, for all of them.

panels.left_bubble: Whose computer, though?
panels.right_bubble: I'd start with Frappe Cloud, the official hosting for Frappe apps. It installs, upgrades and watches over the system.

panels.left_bubble: And if we leave ERPNext for good? Do our records come with us?
panels.right_bubble: Yes. Frappe Cloud lets you download a full backup any time. Moving it elsewhere is still work.
One catch. Hosting runs the system. It doesn't set it up around how you work. You still need good people.

panels.left_bubble: So Frappe earns from the help, not the code.
panels.right_bubble: Yes. Frappe and its partners are paid for setup, hosting and support. Costs get their own chapter.

panels.left_bubble: Open, with good people. Proven, for now.
panels.right_bubble: I'll take 'for now' from you.

panels.left_bubble: ERPNext, and a cloud to run it. What else does Frappe make?

explainers.title: Everything Frappe makes
explainers.takeaway: Apps for each job, one toolkit under them, one cloud to run them.
explainers.dek: Joseph wants the whole map: apps for each job, the toolkit they are built on, and the cloud they run on.
explainers.so_far: ERPNext is open, nobody can lock you in, and Frappe Cloud can run it.

panels.caption: So far: ERPNext is open, nobody can lock you in, and Frappe Cloud can run it. Joseph keeps the laptops, the phones and every sheet that breaks.

panels.left_bubble: Before anyone picks anything, I want the whole map. Is Frappe one app, or a family?

panels.right_bubble: A family. An app is software for one job. ERPNext is one of them.

panels.caption: Raju's customers: Frappe CRM.
Salman's cafe complaints: Frappe Helpdesk.
Ishita's payroll: Frappe HR.
CRM: software that keeps track of every customer and lead.
panels.left_bubble: A CRM? I keep every customer up here!
Hello? Sorry, which cafe wanted the decaf?

panels.caption: Apps for running a business, one job each.
panels.diagram_labels:
# For running a business
- ERPNext: accounts, stock, sales
- Frappe CRM: customers
- Frappe Helpdesk: complaints
- Frappe HR: people, payroll
- Learning: online courses
- Insights: dashboards, reports
- Lending: loans
- Raven: team chat

panels.left_bubble: And what are all these apps built with?

panels.right_bubble: A toolkit for building business apps: the Frappe Framework. ERPNext was the first app built with it.
Like your roaster: one machine, many different roasts.

panels.left_bubble: So ERPNext is the house blend.
Which came first, the roaster or the blend?
panels.right_bubble: The roaster. They built the Framework so they could build ERPNext.

panels.left_bubble: So how would The Coffee Company actually get these apps?

panels.right_bubble: On Frappe Cloud you get a site: your company's own copy, at its own web address.

panels.caption: One site can hold several apps.
panels.diagram_labels:
# thecoffeecompany.m.frappe.cloud
- ERPNext
- Frappe CRM
- More apps, later

panels.left_bubble: So we install everything on day one?
panels.right_bubble: No. Having many apps doesn't mean each fits you. Check each one against how you work.

panels.left_bubble: So it's Frappe all the way down.
panels.right_bubble: Pretty much: every app sits on the same toolkit.

panels.left_bubble: Enough about the company. What does ERPNext actually do for us?
panels.right_bubble: That's next: how one cafe order becomes an invoice.
